Hi Sara — great questions, thanks for the clear list. Short answer up front: tokens are metered consistently in the hosted product (we charge per billed token), but there are a few operational differences between APIs that can affect the effective tokens billed for a call. Below I mapped the key distinctions and included a tiny worked example.

Summary (TL;DR):
- Base metering: request + response tokens are added and billed per the same tokenization rules across Chat and Responses. Legacy endpoints may have additional per-call overhead for certain older model wrappers.
- Streaming: billed tokens reflect the full response produced; streaming doesn't reduce billed tokens, it only affects delivery latency.
- Practical differences: Chat-style endpoints include role tokens (system/user/assistant) in the request token count; Responses API flattens some metadata which can make the request token count slightly lower for equivalent payloads. Legacy endpoints sometimes add fixed wrapper bytes which can show up as a small per-request delta.

Worked example (approx):
- Prompt (user): 30 tokens
- System instructions: 40 tokens
- Model response: 220 tokens
Billed tokens = 30 + 40 + 220 = 290 (hosted token unit).

Where you might see variance:
- Chat endpoint: role prefixes ("user:/assistant:") are tokenized; if you send long system messages, you'll see that included.
- Responses API: we recommend passing structured metadata in the metadata field rather than concatenating into system messages — that often reduces request tokens.
- Legacy endpoints: some older wrappers include JSON envelope padding; per-call overhead is typically ~5-20 tokens depending on model and payload.

Attachments: I've attached our latest public ratecard v3 (redwood_ratecard_v3.pdf) — see the "Metering & Units" section for tables and examples. For your forecasting, assume parity in token unit pricing but add a small buffer (we usually recommend 3-5%) if you expect heavy use of legacy calls.

If helpful, I can run three quick sample calls with your representative prompts and send back exact token counts.

Best,
Evelyn Hart

Sara/Evelyn — adding a couple of pricing notes from the commercial side so NeoFlow can incorporate into the model: 

1) List price parity: our hosted per-token list price is consistent regardless of endpoint family for the same model family. That means the unit price you see in the ratecard applies to Chat, Responses, and legacy endpoints.
2) Minimum-billing / per-call charges: for very small payloads (<10 billed tokens) some legacy integrations historically showed a per-call floor in our internal telemetry; we do not surface a separate per-call surcharge on invoices but small calls can appear noisier in aggregated forecasts.
3) Discounts: for committed hosted usage we can apply a volume discount that reduces the per-token rate across endpoints. For NeoFlow's expected volumes (per your note in HubSpot), I can draft a simple committed-use discount schedule and model the effective blended rate across your projected mix (Chat-heavy vs Responses-heavy).

Ben
Director, Commercial Operations | Redwood Inference

P.S. Dev — can you add a short example to the public docs that shows a 3-call comparison (Chat/Responses/Legacy) with identical prompt so customers can see token deltas?

Thanks team — Sara, per Ben's note we put together the sample run and a short FAQ entry. See below for the three-call transcript and exact token counts we measured using your sample prompt (attached as small CSV in Drive link).

Measured example (exact token counts from our test harness):
- Chat endpoint (v1/chat/completions): request 72 tokens (incl. role tokens), response 198 tokens => billed 270 tokens.
- Responses API (v1/responses): request 64 tokens (metadata field used), response 198 tokens => billed 262 tokens.
- Legacy endpoint (v0/legacy/generate): request 74 tokens (wrapper padding), response 198 tokens => billed 272 tokens.

Net takeaway: differences are small on a per-call basis (<5%), but they add up at scale. For forecasting: use the Responses API numbers if you adopt the metadata approach; otherwise assume Chat parity. Ben will follow up with a committed-use quote that shows blended pricing across projected call mix.
